stocks.note: Numbers as of market close on July 22nd.
stocks.news:
Stocks slipped as earnings season rolled on. The NASDAQ gave back 0.57% to 25,690, the S&P 500 eased 0.14% to 7,498, and the DOW was basically flat, off 0.01% to 52,218.

The headliners reported after the bell. Google beat on profit but told investors it needs to spend even more on AI to hit its goals. Tesla grew sales yet watched profit sink under heavy AI and robotics spending. IBM missed and fell again on fears it is behind in the AI race. Their 2026 paths could hardly look more different (chart below): Alphabet is up about 9% on the year, Tesla is down about 17%, and IBM has lost roughly 31%. Elsewhere, AMD said it will pour $5 billion into AI startup Anthropic, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia signed a deal to sell American nuclear technology to the kingdom, and EU regulators cleared the $110 billion Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger with strings attached.

feature_image.alt: Line chart of 2026 year-to-date price returns for Alphabet, Tesla, and IBM through July 22, 2026. Alphabet ends up 9.29%, Tesla down 16.83%, and IBM down 30.53%.
feature_image.caption: Three very different 2026s. Alphabet is up about 9% year to date, Tesla is down about 17%, and IBM has lost roughly 31%, all through July 22, the day the three reported earnings.
feature_image.source: Source: Google Finance. YTD price return through July 22, 2026.

economy.note: Gold and silver are live spot quotes taken the morning of July 23 (change versus the same time a day earlier); the 10-Year, Brent, stocks, and crypto are as of the July 22 close. Metals can move fast intraday, so treat these as a morning snapshot.
economy.commentary:
Retiring is getting more expensive. Fidelity now estimates a 65-year-old leaving the workforce in 2026 will spend an average of about $185,500 on healthcare in retirement, and this year's estimate jumped roughly 7%, the biggest one-year increase in the series (chart below). Long-term care is not even in that number.

Oil kept climbing. Brent crude rose 1.85% to $95.85 as Middle East supply worries lingered. The 10-Year Treasury held at 4.65%.

The metals cooled off. Gold slipped back below $4,100, down about 2.1% to $4,046, and silver fell roughly 3.2% to $57.90 after a strong run, as traders booked profits and weighed the odds of Fed cuts.

Why a REALTOR® cares about retiree healthcare: it is one more fixed cost competing for the same dollars as a mortgage. For move-up sellers and downsizing retirees especially, a bigger medical reserve can change how much house makes sense.

feature_image.alt: Line chart of the year-over-year percent change in Fidelity's annual retiree health care cost estimate from 2018 to 2026, rising to a series-high jump of about 7% in 2026.
feature_image.caption: Fidelity's annual retiree health care cost estimate jumped about 7% this year, the biggest one-year increase in the series. A 65-year-old retiring in 2026 now faces an average of roughly $185,500 in lifetime medical costs, and that excludes long-term care.
feature_image.source: Source: Fidelity Investments 2026 Retiree Health Care Cost Estimate.

crypto.note: Numbers as of 4:00 PM ET, July 22nd.
crypto.commentary:
Crypto drifted lower. Bitcoin eased 0.47% to $65,779, Ether slipped 0.29% to $1,927, and XRP edged up 0.30% to $1.14.

The news was about the rules. A new Senate bill would bar the president and top federal officials from launching or endorsing any cryptocurrency, an update tucked into the still-unsigned Clarity Act, after recent political crypto ventures raised conflict of interest questions. Separately, federal agents clawed back more than $25 million in crypto from scammers running fake romance and investment schemes, a reminder that if an online sweetheart is asking for Bitcoin, it is probably not love.

real_estate.homebuilder: The 30-Year Jumps To 6.85%, Its Highest Since Last June, But Sellers Are Cutting Prices; Locally, 741 Homes Remain Buyable Across Our Five Cities
real_estate.commentary:
The daily 30-year fixed jumped to 6.85%, its highest since June of last year, and the 15-year rose to 6.29%. Rates have been grinding higher alongside oil and inflation worries.

Here is the twist: buyers are not all backing down. With rates up, plenty of sellers are trimming asking prices and more homes are hitting the market, which hands buyers real room to negotiate. The affordability math is still brutal, though. The ICE Mortgage Technology index suggests it would take about a 16% drop in home prices, a 19% jump in incomes, or mortgage rates back near 5% to get affordability back to normal, and none of those is coming soon. So the opportunity right now is less about cheaper prices and more about less competition and more willing sellers.
